Adr.description:
An architecture decision record.

Carries no relationship properties of its own: an ADR's connections to

BlueprintKind.description:
Whether a blueprint documents one concrete element or a pattern that

CheckOutcome.description:
What became of one check in a run.

A run reports an outcome for every check it knows about, including the
ones it was not asked to perform, because the alternative — omitting
them — leaves a consumer unable to tell a check that passed from a check
that never ran.

CheckResult.description: The outcome of one check in a run.

reason.description:
Why the check could not run, present exactly when `outcome` is
`unverified`.

rule.description: The check this result is for.

ComponentBlueprint.description:
A C4 component blueprint: a single component promoted out of its
parent's roster into a document of its own, because it warrants more
than a record block.

Carries no parent property. A component has exactly one parent, as C4
requires, and its parent's roster section already links it by
`[[slug]]` under its own heading — so the edge is declared once, in the
one place a reader meets the child, and the index derives the component's
parent from that inbound link. `contained_by` is the module level's
alone, because being composed into more than one container is what
distinguishes a module from a component.

contracts_consumed.description:
Contract slugs this element depends on.

Named contracts only. An element's untyped collaborators are not
listed here — those are neighbour edges, and per ADR-009 they belong
to the parent that composes the elements, or to the code.

ContainerBlueprint.description:
A C4 container blueprint: one independently deployable or runnable
artifact.

The modules and components composed into it are not listed here, and
the two arrive by different routes. A module names its hosts itself, in
`contained_by`, because a module may be composed into several containers
and that set is a fact about the module. A component has exactly one
parent, as C4 requires, and that edge is recorded where a reader meets
it: the Components section of this document's body, where each child is
a fenced record block XOR a `[[slug]]` blueprint link under its own
heading, per ADR-008 and ADR-012. Either way the index derives this
container's roster rather than reading it from frontmatter.

ContentHash.description:
A digest over a criterion's content, written as `sha256:` followed by
lowercase hexadecimal.

What is hashed is the criterion's name and text and nothing else. Source
positions and parser node identifiers are excluded on purpose — node
identifiers are positional counters that shift whenever anything above
them is edited, and a criterion that moved has not changed.

This is what makes "which criteria changed since the last index" a
comparison of records rather than a diff of markdown.

Contract.description:
An interface specification governing an exchange across a boundary of
independent change.

consumers.description:
Known consumers, by slug. Derived knowledge rather than a
restriction — an unlisted consumer is not forbidden, it is merely
unknown to the provider.

provider.description:
The container or system that provides this interface.

version.description:
The contract's semantic version.

Required rather than optional: a contract without a version cannot
state a compatibility promise, which is the only reason to write one
down separately from the code that implements it.

visibility.description:
Whether this interface is published beyond the repository that
declares it, and therefore whether its versioning policy binds
adopters outside this team.

ContractEdges.description:
The contract edges a C4 element owns: the interfaces it publishes, and
the interfaces it depends on.

Declared once and inherited by all four blueprint types rather than
repeated on each, because the same fact recorded at four altitudes
under three different spellings is how a vocabulary drifts. An element
provides a contract at whichever altitude it happens to sit; the
property is named for the concept, not for the level.

These are not the neighbour edges ADR-009 reserves to a parent. A
neighbour relationship varies by host — a shared module has different
collaborators in every container that composes it, which is why no
single outward list is correct and the parent owns it. A contract is a
named document with one identity, and the fact that an element
publishes or depends on it holds wherever that element is composed. So
this edge belongs to the element, and ADR-009's rule is untouched.

listed here — those are neighbour edges, and per ADR-009 they belong
to the parent that composes the elements, or to the code.

contracts_provided.description:

The interface is this element's own, so it is recorded here whatever
the element's altitude — a system's public API, a container's
service surface, a module's package API, a component's interface
where it warrants a contract document of its own.

ConventionsConfig.description:
House conventions an adopting repository may set, and the profile
supplies when it does not.

line_width.description:
The maximum width of a prose line, measured in Unicode codepoints
rather than bytes, so an em dash counts as one character and not as
its three UTF-8 bytes.

Lines inside fenced code blocks, table rows, and lines containing a
URL are exempt. Defaults to the active profile's registered value.

Criterion.description:
One acceptance criterion.

**The criterion is the atomic unit.** Its body is carried as text rather
than decomposed into steps and example rows, and that is a deliberate
narrowing of an earlier design.

Decomposition would model one notation. Steps typed by role and example
rows keyed by a header are recoverable from Gherkin and from almost
nothing else: a prose criterion has no steps to type, so those properties
would sit empty for every criterion the corpus has not yet migrated, and
populating them from any other notation would need inference rather than
parsing. A model that only one notation can fill is a model of that
notation.

Nothing this framework does today operates below the level of a whole
criterion. Queries fetch one by identifier, change detection compares
hashes, validation reads tags. Decomposition is additive if a consumer
ever needs it — the index schema grows without a breaking change — and
removing it later would not be.

content_hash.description:
A hash of the criterion's name and text, excluding its position.

Two indexes of the same criterion agree on this value whether or not the
criterion moved; they disagree the moment its wording changes.

description.description:
Rationale attached to this criterion alone, absent where none was
written.

Normative statements do not belong here; prose in this position is
reported as a probable untagged criterion rather than recorded as
requirement text.

id.description: The criterion's identifier, from the tag that declares it.

level.description:
The level at which the criterion is intended to be verified, absent
where the author declared none.

manual.description:
Whether the criterion can only be verified by hand.

A criterion marked this way is exempt from the obligation that some test
cite it.

name.description:
The criterion's name — the text following the `Scenario`,
`Scenario Outline` or `Examples` keyword that declares it.

Absent for a notation that gives a criterion no name, as prose does.

negative.description:
Whether the criterion states a prohibition.

Carried as its own property because a prohibition loses its grammatical
marking in Gherkin: where prose wrote `SHALL NOT`, a scenario writes an
ordinary sentence, and the fact that it forbids rather than requires
would otherwise be unrecoverable from the record.

notation.description: The notation this criterion was written in.

position.description:
Where in its document the criterion is written, as a span rather than a
bare line number, so that a report and a rewrite both address the
criterion itself.

rule.description:
The name of the business rule this criterion sits beneath, absent where
it sits directly under its feature.

The rule's name is an assertion — "a build failure is the checker's job,
not the indexer's" — so recording it puts the reason several criteria
exist together in the index, scoped explicitly rather than inferred from
position in a document.

text.description:
The criterion's body, exactly as written.

For a Gherkin criterion this is its steps and any example table,
verbatim, with the block's common indentation removed. For a prose
criterion it is the sentence. One property serves both because the
criterion is the unit, and its text is what every notation has.

CriterionId.description:
The identifier of one acceptance criterion, as written in the tag that
declares it.

Constrained here rather than checked in code, because this is the join
between three things that must agree: the criterion in a specification,
the citation a test carries, and the row a central store holds. The
pattern is the one the framework's acceptance-criterion traceability
standard already fixes, minus
the leading `@` that makes it a Gherkin tag — the identifier is the
value, and the tag is only how it is written down.

The middle segments are the owning feature's code and number, which is
what allows a criterion to name its feature without carrying a second
property: `AC-GHK-001.1` belongs to the feature coded `GHK` numbered
`001`.

CriterionNotation.description:
The notation a criterion was written in.

Recorded on every criterion rather than assumed for the corpus, because
the notation is a replaceable input and a consumer should branch on a
stated value rather than on which properties happen to be populated.

This framework's extractor emits `gherkin` only — nothing reads a prose
criterion. The second value is what keeps the property meaningful: a
one-value enum states nothing, and a record that came from a migration
snapshot or another producer needs somewhere to say so.

Delivery.description: The delivery unit a feature blueprint is groomed against.

DocumentFrontmatter.description:
The metadata envelope every specification document carries.

Membership in the corpus is determined by this envelope rather than by
location: a markdown file whose frontmatter parses and declares a known
`type` is a specification, wherever it sits in the tree. Each document
type extends this struct with its own relationship and classification
properties, so the envelope is validated identically everywhere and only
the extension differs.

A relationship property here or on any extension is declared at one end
only; the index derives the reverse from every other document's inbound
edges. Before adding one, check it against the Document Relationship
Standard — a property that merely mirrors the document's own prose
citations does not earn its maintenance cost.

DocumentType.description:
The classification of a specification document.

A document's type selects the schema, slug pattern and required sections
that govern it. This is the controlled vocabulary the spec-driven-dev
profile registers; a repository whose documents declare a type outside
this set is recorded as excluded with reason `unknown-type` rather than
being checked against the wrong rules.

DocumentTypeRegistration.description: Everything the engine needs to check one document type.

numbered.description:
Whether documents of this type carry a sequence number the CLI can
derive the next value of.

Numbering is global per type: the next number is one greater than the
highest in use anywhere in the corpus, regardless of directory.

pairings.description: Relationship properties that must be declared from both ends.

reference_properties.description:
Frontmatter properties of this type that hold document references.

A value in one of these properties that matches no corpus member's
slug is reported the same way an unresolved `[[slug]]` in the body is.

schema.description:
The JSON Schema this type's frontmatter is validated against,
expressed as a JSON Pointer into the bundled schema or as a path to a
standalone one.

section_sets.description:
Named sets of headings a span query can select, so a reviewing agent
can ask for the normative sections of a document and read only those.

sections.description: The heading hierarchy a document of this type must contain.

slug_pattern.description:
The pattern a document of this type must match in its `slug`.

A mismatch is reported with both the actual slug and this pattern
quoted, so the finding is self-contained and the fixing agent needs no
further lookup.

typed_reference_properties.description:
Reference-bearing properties whose target must declare a particular
document `type`, keyed by property name with the required type as the
value.

A schema can require that `frd` holds exactly one slug; only the index
knows what that slug resolves to, so the type half of the constraint is
registered here. Every key must also appear in `reference_properties`
— a typed property that is not reference-bearing would be checked
against a target nothing resolved.

ElementRecord.description:
The three fields that identify any element the framework names.

This is the smallest unit of description in the vocabulary, and it is
deliberately shared by two artifacts that look unrelated. A child element
a parent document declares inline — a component of a container, a module
of a system — carries exactly these fields in a fenced record block. A
child that has been promoted to its own document carries them as the
opening of its frontmatter, because `DocumentFrontmatter` inherits them.

One schema therefore validates a child in either state, which is what
makes promotion a lift-and-link operation rather than a re-authoring
one: the record block moves verbatim into the new document's
frontmatter, and every parent roster replaces the block with a link.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

The identifier every other document uses to reference this element.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and

title.description:
Human-readable title. Free text.

On a promoted document this is also the document's H1, and the two are
kept in sync by hand.

ExclusionReason.description:
Why a candidate file beneath the spec root is not a corpus member.

Exclusions are recorded rather than dropped, so that a document which
*should* be a specification but is missing frontmatter is visible in the
index rather than absent from it — a judgement the tool cannot make for
the reader.

Feature.description:
One feature, extracted from a fenced Gherkin block or a standalone
feature file.

A feature is the unit a requirement maps onto: one cohesive capability,
independently testable, with its own code and slug. Its criteria are
nested beneath it because that is what they are — a criterion has no
meaning apart from the feature it qualifies, and the containment is the
data's own shape rather than an index's convenience.

Lookup does not need the collection flattened. An acceptance-criterion
identifier carries its feature's code, so resolving a criterion to its
feature is reading the identifier, and resolving an identifier to a
criterion is one index built over this tree when the index is read.

code.description:
The code the identifier groups this feature under, recorded so that a
consumer selecting a group does not have to split the identifier.

criteria.description:
The feature's acceptance criteria, in the order they are written.

Nested rather than held in a sibling collection. A criterion belongs to
exactly one feature, its identifier already names which, and a consumer
fetching a feature wants its criteria with it.

description.description:
The feature's description: its user story, and any design note or scope
fence written beneath it.

Absent where none was written, which is reported as a caution rather
than a failure — a feature with no story is legible but poorer, and
refusing to index it would help nobody.

document_slug.description:
The slug of the document that owns this feature.

Populated for both source forms, but established differently: a fenced
block inherits the slug of the document it is written in, and a
standalone feature file — being no document — names its owner in a tag.
Derivation is preferred wherever it is available, so that the record
cannot disagree with the document holding it.

id.description:
The feature's identifier — its durable address, carrying the group code
and the number that distinguishes it within that group.

name.description: The feature's name — the text following the `Feature` keyword.

path.description:
The path of the file the feature is written in, relative to the
repository root and written with forward slashes on every platform.

position.description:
Where in its file the feature is written, as a span covering the Gherkin
itself.

For a feature written as a fenced block, this covers the Gherkin inside
the fence; the fence's own extent is carried by `source`.

source.description: Which admissible form the feature was written in.

FeatureBlueprint.description:
A transient change document describing how the system changes to deliver
one feature.

Unlike the blueprints it modifies, a feature blueprint describes a
change rather than a state, so it reaches `in-progress` and then
`retired` rather than `active`.

The documents the change creates and updates are described in the
blueprint's own "Documentation Changes" prose and tracked to completion
in its `plan`, which records done-ness natively. They are not mirrored
into frontmatter: a change set recorded in three places is three places
that must agree.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

delivery.description:
The delivery unit grooming plans against. When `staged`, each stage
boundary is enumerated in the blueprint's Sequencing Constraints.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

frd.description:
The FRD this blueprint realizes, one to one.

A feature blueprint answers how the system changes; the FRD it names
answers what the change must achieve. Singular and required, so the
one-to-one relationship is expressible in the schema rather than only
in this comment, and named `frd` rather than `sources` so that one
property name does not span two relationships — `Frd.sources` is
optional, many-valued provenance, which is a different edge.

plan.description:
Where this feature's implementation plan lives, stamped in by the
groom-feature-blueprint skill once grooming serializes the plan:
an epic id (`agent-plugins-bge`) when the plan is beads, or a
repository-relative directory (`plans/<feature-slug>/`) when it is
task files. Absent before grooming, since an ungroomed blueprint has
no plan yet; present through `retired`, since the pointer retires
with the document rather than being cleared.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and
conventionally prefixed by the document type — `adr-013`,
`container-spec-cli`, `module-document-core`.

FeatureCode.description:
The short code that groups features by topic, domain or capability.

Uppercase and terse — `GHK`, `SPEC`, `CHK`. **Features share a code**:
`SPEC` covers eleven requirements of the spec-index feature, and that is
what makes it a grouping rather than an identity. A feature is identified
by its code together with its number.

FeatureId.description:
The identifier of one feature — its prefix, its group code and its number.

`FEAT-SPEC-009`, `FEAT-GHK-001`. This is the feature's durable address: it
does not change when the feature moves between documents or between the
two admissible forms, and it is what every acceptance-criterion identifier
beneath the feature is derived from.

The pattern admits any uppercase prefix rather than fixing `FEAT`, so that
a project adopting the framework can carry its own.

FeatureSource.description:
Which admissible form a feature was written in.

The distinction survives into the index because it changes what a
consumer may do. A fenced block sits inside a document that owns
frontmatter, terminology and references, and rewriting it means editing a
region of markdown. A standalone file has no such document around it and
is the form external tooling ingests directly.

FeatureSourceBlock.description: A feature written as a fenced Gherkin block inside a markdown document.

block.description:
The extent of the fenced block, opening and closing fences included.

Recorded because the feature's own span covers the Gherkin inside the
fence, and a caller that replaces or extracts the whole construct needs
the fence too. This is the same distinction the framework's region
scanner already draws between an inner and an outer extent.

FeatureSourceFile.description:
A feature written as a standalone `.feature` file.

Carries nothing of its own. The file is the feature, so its path is
already on the feature and its extent is the whole document; this shape
exists so the source form is a value a consumer branches on rather than
one it infers from the absence of another property.

FeatureTagRegistration.description:
The tags a profile assigns meaning to on a feature and its criteria.

Which tag identifies a feature, which identifies a criterion, which
prefix names the document a feature belongs to, and which qualifiers
carry meaning are facts about a document vocabulary rather than about
Gherkin. They are registered here so that the engine reads a tag as a
string and attaches meaning to none of it.

Every member is optional and a profile MAY register none of them. A
partial registration is honest rather than defective: a profile that
identifies features and not criteria has a corpus with no criteria in
it.

criterion_pattern.description:
The pattern the identifier of an acceptance criterion matches, without
the leading marker that makes it a tag.

feature_pattern.description:
The pattern the identifier of a feature matches, without the leading
marker that makes it a tag.

Named capture groups in this pattern are what `shared_captures`
selects from, so a profile that derives criterion identifiers from
feature identifiers names the shared parts here.

owner_prefix.description:
The prefix carried by the tag in which a feature names the document
that owns it, where the feature is not written inside that document.

A feature written as a standalone file has no frontmatter to inherit
an owner from, so it names one in a tag; the prefix is what
distinguishes that tag from every other tag on the feature.

qualifiers.description: The tags that qualify a criterion, and what each of them means.

shared_captures.description:
The named capture groups a criterion identifier shares with the
identifier of the feature it belongs to.

This is how a criterion identifier's derivation from its feature's is
stated without the engine knowing the internal structure of either
pattern: it compiles both, captures both identifiers, and compares
only the groups named here. Every name must be a capture group both
patterns define.

Finding.description:
One reported conformance result.

Every check in this tool reports through this shape, so a consumer
renders one thing and a check added later is readable by a consumer
written before it. The five common properties are what make a diagnostic
self-contained — the rule that raised it, how badly it bears on the run,
which file, where in that file, and what is wrong — and `detail` carries
the same information again in structured form for a consumer that acts
on it rather than printing it.

detail.description: The structured form of the same defect.

message.description:
What is wrong, stating the violated constraint and the value that
violated it, so the finding needs no further lookup to act on.

path.description:
The file the finding is against, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

position.description:
Where in the file the finding is, as a span rather than a bare line
number, so a report can point at a value inside a line.

rule.description: The check that raised this finding.

severity.description: How badly this finding bears on the run.

FindingDetail.description:
The structured detail of one finding, selected by the kind of defect.

Every finding carries one. The message on the finding is derivable from
this value, so a consumer branches on structure rather than parsing
prose, and a renderer that wants to offer a fix reads the fields it needs
as values.

The union is open to extension in the sense that matters: a later check
adds a variant without changing the envelope that carries it, and a
consumer that does not recognise a variant still has the rule
identifier, the severity, the path, the span and the message.

FindingDuplicateIdentifier.description:
An identifier declared by more than one record in the corpus.

Reported against each of the two records, each naming the other, so that
checking either one surfaces the collision. The other occurrence's span
is carried alongside its path because a file holds many records and an
identifier is not a heading: without the span the reader is told which
file to open and left to search it.

other_path.description:
The other occurrence's path, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

other_position.description: Where in that file the other occurrence is written.

FindingDuplicateSlug.description:
A slug declared by more than one corpus member.

Reported against each of the two documents, each naming the other, so
that checking either one surfaces the collision.

other_path.description:
The other document's path, relative to the repository root and written
with forward slashes on every platform.

slug.description: The slug both documents declare.

FindingFrontmatterParse.description:
A frontmatter block that could not be read as a document envelope.

Distinct from a schema violation, and reported by a different route: a
schema violation is found by validating a parsed envelope, while this is
what happens when there is no parsed envelope to validate. The document
declared itself a specification and got the declaration wrong badly
enough that nothing downstream can look at it.

Modelled separately because it is the one finding that suppresses all
the others for its document. A consumer must be able to tell "this
document passed every check" from "no check could run against this
document", and the rule identifier alone does not carry that: the other
checks report `passed` for a document they never examined unless
something says otherwise.

message.description:
What could not be read, quoted from the parser so the message needs no
further lookup to act on.

FindingGherkinParse.description:
A Gherkin source that could not be parsed.

Held apart from a frontmatter parse failure because the two are found by
different readers and fixed in different places: a Gherkin source sits
inside a document whose envelope parsed perfectly well, and only the
feature it declares is lost. The parser's own expectation is carried so
that the author is told what was admissible at that position rather than
only that something was not.

expected.description:
What the parser expected at the offending position, quoted from the
parser so the message needs no further lookup to act on.

FindingIdentifierPattern.description:
A record whose identifier tag is absent or does not match the pattern
registered for it.

One shape for both defects, because the fix is the same act — write a
conforming identifier — and the two are told apart by the rule that
raised the finding. The pattern is carried in either case: an author who
wrote no identifier needs to know the form of the one to write just as
much as an author who wrote a wrong one.

identifier.description:
The identifier as written, absent where the record carries no
identifier tag at all.

pattern.description: The pattern the active profile registers for identifiers of this kind.

FindingIncompletePairing.description:
One half of a paired relationship the counterpart does not declare.

Reported against both documents, each carrying this same detail, so that
checking either one surfaces the half-built edge and the two copies
describe the relationship in the same direction rather than each from its
own point of view.

counterpart.description:
The property the referenced document must declare in return, and does
not.

property.description: The reference-bearing property the referring document declares.

source_path.description:
The referring document's path, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

target_path.description:
The referenced document's path, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

FindingMissingProperty.description:
A property the document's type requires and the document does not
declare.

Modelled apart from the general schema violation because a missing
property is the most common defect by a wide margin, and a consumer
offering to insert one needs the property name as a value rather than as
a substring of a message.

pointer.description: The JSON Pointer of the object that should carry the property.

property.description: The name of the property that is absent.

FindingOwningDocument.description:
A feature whose owning-document tag is absent, names a document other
than the one the feature is written in, or names no corpus member at all.

The three defects share a shape because they share a question — which
document owns this feature — and the rule that raised the finding says
which of them occurred. Both slugs are optional because each defect
leaves a different half unknown: a feature carrying no tag has no slug to
quote, and a standalone feature file is no document and so has none of
its own to disagree with.

document_slug.description:
The slug of the document the feature is written in, absent where the
feature is a standalone feature file rather than a fenced block.

slug.description:
The slug the feature's owning-document tag names, as written, absent
where the feature carries no such tag.

FindingPartiallyTaggedOutline.description:
A scenario outline whose examples blocks are inconsistently tagged: some
carry an identifier and others do not.

The defect is the inconsistency, not the several blocks — an outline
whose blocks are all tagged is several criteria, and one whose blocks are
all untagged is a single criterion written in named groups. Both are
admissible, and the mixture is what no reader can resolve.

The untagged blocks are carried as spans so that a report points at the
blocks to fix rather than at the outline containing them.

untagged.description:
Where each untagged examples block is written, in the order the blocks
occur.

FindingReferenceType.description:
A typed reference whose target declares a document type other than the
one the active profile requires for that property.

A frontmatter schema can require that a property holds exactly one slug;
only the index knows what that slug resolves to, so the type half of the
constraint is checked here and reported with both types quoted.

expected_type.description: The document `type` the active profile requires the target to declare.

property.description: The reference-bearing property whose target's type is constrained.

slug.description: The slug the property names.

FindingReport.description:
Everything one check run produced.

The two collections answer different questions and neither substitutes
for the other. `findings` is what is wrong; `checks` is what was looked
at. A report carrying no findings is only good news if every check the
caller cares about is accounted for in `checks` as having passed.

Both are lists rather than maps so that the emitter owns their order and
can make output byte-identical across platforms without a change to this
model.

checks.description:
Every check the run knows about, in the order the emitter fixes, each
with what became of it.

findings.description: Every finding the run produced, in the order the emitter fixes.

FindingRetiredTarget.description:
A reference from a live document to one the active profile treats as
retired.

The target resolves — the reader reaches a real document that says it has
been replaced — so this is a warning rather than an error. The successor
is what makes it worth reporting at all: it is the one finding that tells
an author what to cite instead.

slug.description: The retired target's slug.

successor.description:
The replacement the retired target names, read from the property the
active profile registers for that purpose.

Absent where the target declares none. Not every retirement has a
successor, and a finding that implied otherwise would send the reader
looking for one.

FindingSchemaViolation.description:
A frontmatter value that violates the schema its document type is
validated against.

The pointer and the constraint together make the finding actionable
without re-running the validator: the pointer says which property, and
the constraint says what it had to satisfy.

constraint.description: The constraint the value failed, quoted as the schema states it.

pointer.description:
The JSON Pointer at which the violation occurred, relative to the
document's frontmatter.

value.description:
The offending value, as raw source text rather than as a YAML parser
reinterpreted it, so a date written unquoted is reported as it was
written.

FindingSlugPattern.description:
A slug that does not match the pattern the active profile supplies for
the document's type.

Both halves are carried so the finding is self-contained: an agent
fixing it needs neither the profile nor the document open.

pattern.description: The pattern the active profile supplies for this document's type.

slug.description: The slug the document declares.

FindingUnmappedCitation.description:
A citation whose slug names a corpus document the caller's link map does
not cover.

Distinct from `FindingUnresolvedCitation`: the slug does resolve to a
real corpus document, so the defect is a gap in the map rather than a
bad citation, and the fix is to add the missing entry rather than to fix
the prose. The map's path is carried alongside the slug and the citing
document so the finding is actionable without the caller having the map
open.

citing_path.description:
The citing document's path, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

map_path.description:
The link map's path, relative to the repository root and written with
forward slashes on every platform.

slug.description: The slug the citation names.

FindingUnresolvedCitation.description:
A citation whose slug names no corpus document at all.

Distinct from `FindingUnmappedCitation`: nothing in the corpus resolves
the slug, so the citation is as likely to be illustrative prose — a
template teaching citation syntax — as a mistyped reference, and the two
cannot be told apart by the tool. Carrying only the slug and the citing
document (no map path) reflects that a link map, present or absent, is
not what decided this outcome.

citing_path.description:
The citing document's path, relative to the repository root and
written with forward slashes on every platform.

slug.description: The slug the citation names.

FindingUnresolvedReference.description:
A reference that reached no corpus member.

The origin is carried because it decides how the defect reads: a `[[…]]`
in prose is quoted back, while a value in a registered frontmatter
property is reported by naming the property that holds it. The
non-member half is carried because a slug that matched a file the index
excluded or could not parse is a different problem with a different fix,
and telling the reader which one they have saves them a search for a
document that is right there.

non_member.description:
The non-member file the slug matched, with the reason it is not a
member.

Absent when the slug matched nothing at all, which is the ordinary
case; present when the target exists beneath the spec root and is
excluded or unparsable.

origin.description:
Where the reference was written: the document's body, or a named
reference-bearing frontmatter property.

slug.description:
The slug half of the reference, as written — everything before the
first `#`, whose anchor half is not part of this defect.

FindingUnverified.description:
A check that was requested and could not run.

This is the structured half of the `unverified` severity: the reason
states what was missing, so a consumer can decide whether to install a
dependency, adjust configuration, or accept the gap.

reason.description:
Why the check could not run, stated so that it needs no further lookup
to act on.

Frd.description:
A feature requirements document: the user need, its scope boundaries and
the acceptance criteria that decide whether it has been met.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

slug.description:
The identifier every other document uses to reference this element.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and
conventionally prefixed by the document type — `adr-013`,
`container-spec-cli`, `module-document-core`.

sources.description:
The documents this FRD is derived from — a brief, a research
document, or an FRD it narrows.

superseded_by.description:
The document that replaces this one.

Required in practice on any document at `status: retired` — a retired
document with no resolvable successor is a dead end for anyone who
follows a reference to it.

tags.description: Free-form tags for filtering and search.

title.description:
Human-readable title. Free text.

On a promoted document this is also the document's H1, and the two are
kept in sync by hand.

type.description:
The document's classification, which selects the schema, slug pattern
and required sections that govern it.

updated_at.description:
RFC 3339 timestamp of the last substantive modification.

Validated against the text as written in the file rather than against
a parsed value, so a bare `2026-07-29` is reported as a defect instead
of being silently widened to midnight UTC by the YAML parser.

Guide.description:
A how-to document explaining a technique that other document types
assume knowledge of — EARS syntax, C4 mapping, cross-document reference
conventions.

A guide carries no relationships of its own: it explains a technique
rather than participating in the architecture graph.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

slug.description:
The identifier every other document uses to reference this element.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and
conventionally prefixed by the document type — `adr-013`,
`container-spec-cli`, `module-document-core`.

superseded_by.description:
The document that replaces this one.

Required in practice on any document at `status: retired` — a retired
document with no resolvable successor is a dead end for anyone who

tags.description: Free-form tags for filtering and search.

title.description:
Human-readable title. Free text.

On a promoted document this is also the document's H1, and the two are
kept in sync by hand.

type.description:
The document's classification, which selects the schema, slug pattern
and required sections that govern it.

updated_at.description:
RFC 3339 timestamp of the last substantive modification.

Validated against the text as written in the file rather than against
a parsed value, so a bare `2026-07-29` is reported as a defect instead
of being silently widened to midnight UTC by the YAML parser.

version.description: The guide's semantic version, quoted so YAML reads it as a string.

IndexEntry.description:
One corpus member in the index: where it lives and what its frontmatter
declares.

The entry is deliberately additive. This sprint populates the path and
the frontmatter envelope; later features attach headings, extracted
record blocks and references to the same entry under the same
`schema_version`, and no property here forecloses modelling references
as their own collection later.

frontmatter.description:
The member's parsed frontmatter.

Absent exactly when `parse_error` is present: a document whose
frontmatter could not be parsed is still indexed, but it has no parsed
envelope to carry.

parse_error.description:
The failure that prevented this member's frontmatter from being
parsed, with its position.

Present exactly when `frontmatter` is absent. A member carrying this
property does not make the index a failure; the index is still emitted
and still contains every other document.

path.description:
The member's path, relative to the repository root and written with
forward slashes on every platform.

IndexExclusion.description: One candidate file that is not a corpus member, and why.

path.description:
The excluded file's path, relative to the repository root and written
with forward slashes on every platform.

reason.description: Why the file is not a member.

type.description:
The `type` value the file declared, reported when `reason` is
`unknown-type` so that a reviewing agent can judge whether the profile
or the document is wrong.

ModuleBlueprint.description:
A C4 module blueprint: a coherent unit of code with an interface of its
own, composed into a container.

The components it composes are not listed in frontmatter. Each child is
declared in this document's Components section — a fenced record block
when un-promoted, a `[[slug]]` blueprint link once promoted, exactly one
of the two per ADR-008 — and the index derives the roster from there.

contained_by.description:
The containers, or the modules, that compose this module.

**The only multi-parent relationship in the vocabulary, and the reason
the module level exists.** C4 gives every element exactly one parent —
a container belongs to one system, a component to one container — and
that edge is recorded by the parent, in the roster section of its body.
Module is this framework's addition to C4, and being composed into more
than one container is its whole purpose: a unit shared by two
containers is a module precisely because it is shared.

So this is a list, and it is declared here rather than derived from
parent rosters, because a shared module's hosts are a fact about the
module. It is the direction ADR-009 tells modules to point when it
denies them a context view — no single outward-edge list is correct for
a module, but the set of hosts is, and this is where it goes.

Omitted when no host has a blueprint of its own — absence records a
documented fact rather than an oversight.

contracts_consumed.description:
Contract slugs this element depends on.

Named contracts only. An element's untyped collaborators are not
listed here — those are neighbour edges, and per ADR-009 they belong
to the parent that composes the elements, or to the code.

contracts_provided.description:
Contract slugs this element provides.

The interface is this element's own, so it is recorded here whatever
the element's altitude — a system's public API, a container's
service surface, a module's package API, a component's interface
where it warrants a contract document of its own.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

kind.description:
Whether this blueprint documents one concrete module or a pattern
several modules follow.

slug.description:
The identifier every other document uses to reference this element.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and
conventionally prefixed by the document type — `adr-013`,
`container-spec-cli`, `module-document-core`.

source_paths.description: Repository-relative source roots, so a reader can find the code.

superseded_by.description:
The document that replaces this one.

Required in practice on any document at `status: retired` — a retired
document with no resolvable successor is a dead end for anyone who
follows a reference to it.

tags.description: Free-form tags for filtering and search.

title.description:
Human-readable title. Free text.

On a promoted document this is also the document's H1, and the two are
kept in sync by hand.

type.description:
The document's classification, which selects the schema, slug pattern
and required sections that govern it.

updated_at.description:
RFC 3339 timestamp of the last substantive modification.

Validated against the text as written in the file rather than against
a parsed value, so a bare `2026-07-29` is reported as a defect instead
of being silently widened to midnight UTC by the YAML parser.

version.description:
The module's semantic version.

Required in practice when `visibility` is `public`, since a published
package API owes its consumers a compatibility promise.

visibility.description:
Whether the module is published to a registry, and therefore whether
its package API is bound by a compatibility policy.

ParseError.description:
A located failure to parse part of a document.

Recorded against the document it occurred in rather than raised, because
one unparsable file must not cost a repository the index of every other
file. The position is a `Span`, like every other position this framework
reports.

message.description:
What could not be parsed, stated so that the message needs no further
lookup to act on.

position.description: Where in the document the failure occurred.

name.description:
The name of a registered profile.

Exactly one profile applies per invocation. A value naming no
registered profile is reported as a finding listing the names that are
registered, rather than as a bare startup failure.

ProfileRegistration.description:
What a profile registers into Document Core.

**Internal surface.** This is the vocabulary a profile hands to the
engine in-process, not something an adopting repository authors. It is
not reachable from `specs.toml` in v1 and is not an extension point
outside this repository; `[profile].name` selects one of these
registrations by name, and that naming is the whole of the relationship
between the two halves of the configuration contract.

It is modelled here rather than left to hand-written Go for two
reasons. Registration is data — type names, patterns, section trees,
block tags — and only the rules that cannot be expressed as data stay in
code. And the open question of which internal keys get promoted to the
public surface is answered by editing this struct, which is a smaller
and more reviewable act than editing an interface and its
implementations.

Property names are snake_case throughout, matching the public surface,
so that promoting a key to `specs.toml` is a move rather than a rename.

block_tags.description:
Fenced block info strings whose contents are parsed as structured data
and attached to the containing document and heading.

conventions.description:
The convention values this profile supplies when `specs.toml` omits
them.

document_types.description:
The document types this profile defines, keyed by the value documents
declare in their `type` property.

A markdown file declaring a type absent from this map is recorded as
excluded with reason `unknown-type` and its declared value reported,
so a reviewing agent can judge whether the profile or the document is
wrong.

feature_tags.description:
The tag vocabulary this profile assigns meaning to.

Absent for a profile whose documents carry no tagged features, which
is a corpus without them rather than a malformed registration; the
checks that read it do not run.

finished_statuses.description:
The statuses at which a document is considered finished, and therefore
at which leftover template placeholders are a defect rather than
work in progress.

live_statuses.description:
The statuses at which a document is in effect, and therefore at which a
reference it makes to a retired document is worth reporting.

Profile-level rather than per-type because `status` is a property of
the shared document envelope: every type this profile defines carries
it, and none of them narrows it. A profile registering none of these
three lifecycle keys registers no lifecycle, and the checks that read
them do not run.

name.description: The name an adopting repository writes in `[profile].name`.

placeholder_patterns.description:
Patterns whose presence in a finished document indicates unreplaced
template scaffolding.

retired_statuses.description:
The statuses at which a document is no longer in effect, so that a live
document still pointing at it is reported.

Disjoint from `live_statuses` by construction; a status in neither is
one the lifecycle says nothing about, which is the right answer for a
draft.

successor_property.description:
The name of the frontmatter property in which a retired document names
its replacement.

Registered rather than assumed, because the engine that reports a
retired target must not contain the name of the property this
framework happens to use for it. Its value is quoted back in the
finding, so a reader is told what to cite instead of what they cited.

PropertyPairing.description:
One half of a relationship that must be declared from both ends.

A document naming a counterpart in one property where that counterpart
declares nothing in return is a half-built edge, and it is reported
against both documents rather than only the one that happens to be
checked first.

Reserved for a relationship a reader of one document must see without
consulting the index. Because the index derives the reverse of every
declared edge, a pairing used to enforce a mirror the index already
computes can only ever fail on redundant hand-work — so the
spec-driven-dev profile registers none, and an adopting profile that
registers one is expected to argue the case. See the Document
Relationship Standard.

counterpart.description: The property the referenced document must declare in return.

property.description: The property declared on this document.

QualifierMeaning.description:
What a registered qualifier tag says about the criterion carrying it.

The set is fixed by the criterion record rather than by any profile: a
qualifier can only mean one of the things a criterion has somewhere to
put. A profile chooses the spelling of each tag and which of these
meanings it carries, and nothing else.

QualifierTagRegistration.description:
One tag a profile assigns meaning to on a criterion, and the meaning it
assigns.

A tag absent from this list is carried on the record and reported by
nothing: an unregistered tag is a tag the vocabulary says nothing
about, which is the right answer for an annotation the author added for
their own reasons.

level.description:
The verification level this tag records, for a tag whose meaning is
`verification-level` and for no other.

meaning.description: The property of a criterion this tag populates.

tag.description: The tag, without the leading marker that makes it a tag.

Reference.description:
One occurrence of one document referencing another.

A reference is an edge, and it is recorded as a row of its own rather
than as a property of either document it connects. The facts that make
it actionable — where it was written, whether it came from prose or from
a named frontmatter property, and what it reached — belong to neither
endpoint, and both directions of the graph are derived by indexing this
one collection rather than stored twice.

One row per occurrence. A document that references the same target twice
contributes two rows carrying two spans, so a finding about either cites
the line the reader must open.

anchor.description:
The anchor half: everything after the first `#`, absent where the
reference names no anchor.

Recorded and not interpreted. Resolving an anchor against the target's
headings is a separate feature; splitting on the first `#` is the whole
of what this shape knows about anchors, and it exists so that an
anchored reference resolves on its slug rather than reporting as
broken.

path.description:
The path of the document the reference occurs in, relative to the
repository root and written with forward slashes on every platform.

position.description:
Where in the containing document the reference occurs, as a span rather
than a bare line number, so a report and a rewrite both address the
reference itself.

slug.description:
The slug half: everything before the first `#`, or the whole reference
where it names no anchor.

A plain `String` rather than a `Slug`, deliberately. A reference is
written by hand and may name something that is not a well-formed slug
at all; constraining this property would make such a reference
unrepresentable in the index, which is the one place it must be
visible in order to be reported.

text.description:
The reference exactly as written, without the delimiters that enclose
it — `adr-012`, or `adr-012#Decision`, or the raw value of a
reference-bearing frontmatter property.

Recorded alongside the halves it splits into, because the text is what
a reader sees and what a rewrite replaces, and neither is recoverable
from the halves once letter case or spacing has been normalized.

ReferenceBodyOrigin.description:
A reference written in a document's body.

Carries nothing of its own. What a body reference adds beyond its
position is nothing, and its position is recorded on the reference
itself; this shape exists so that the origin is a value a consumer
branches on rather than a property it has to infer from the absence of
another.

ReferenceFrontmatterOrigin.description:
A reference held by a frontmatter property the active profile registers
as reference-bearing.

property.description:
The name of the frontmatter property the reference was written in, so
that a finding names the property without the document being reopened.

ReferenceNonMember.description:
A reference whose slug matches a file the index recorded as excluded or
as a parse failure rather than as a corpus member.

Held apart from an ordinary unresolved reference because the reader's
next step differs: the document is right there, and what is wrong is its
frontmatter rather than the reference. Exactly one of `reason` and
`parse_error` is present — the two ways a file beneath the spec root
fails to become a member.

parse_error.description:
The failure that prevented the file's frontmatter from being parsed,
with its position, present when the index recorded it as a member
whose frontmatter could not be read.

path.description:
The matched file's path, relative to the repository root and written
with forward slashes on every platform.

reason.description:
Why the file is not a member, present when the index recorded it as an
exclusion.

ReferenceOrigin.description:
Where a reference was written.

The distinction is not decoration. A reference in prose and a reference
in a registered frontmatter property are reported differently — one
quotes the link, the other names the property that holds it — and they
are rewritten differently, so the origin belongs to the reference rather
than being inferred from where its span happens to fall.

ReferenceResolution.description:
What a reference reached.

A reference that reaches nothing is recorded with this state rather than
dropped, because indexing never fails: the index describes the corpus it
found, including the parts of it that are broken, and reporting a broken
reference is a check's job rather than the indexer's.

ReferenceResolved.description: A reference that reached a corpus member.

target_path.description:
The target's path, relative to the repository root and written with
forward slashes on every platform.

The path rather than the slug, because the slug is already on the
reference and a consumer following the edge wants the file.

ReferenceUnresolved.description:
A reference whose slug matches no corpus member and no file the index
knows about at all.

Carries nothing: the slug that matched nothing is already on the
reference this resolution belongs to.

Rfc.description:
An improvement proposal raised against a skill by a run that exercised
it.

The provenance properties below are the load-bearing part. A skill
behaves differently under different models, efforts and harnesses, so a
defect real under one may not reproduce under another, and triage cannot
scope a fix without knowing which run saw it. They are recorded
faithfully by the retro that raises the RFC and judged by the triage
that receives it — the two roles are deliberately separate.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

effort.description:
The reasoning effort the run used.

Left unconstrained because the effort vocabulary belongs to the
harness rather than to this framework, and `unknown` is a legitimate
value when a transcript does not record it.

model.description:
The exact model identifier the run used — not a family name. A finding
that reproduces under one model and not another is scoped by this
property alone.

origin.description:
Where the run happened: `self` when this repository critiqued its own
skill, otherwise the name of the project the run took place in.

plugin_version.description: The plugin version the critiqued skill shipped in.

runs_observed.description:
How many runs stand behind the evidence.

This is the denominator for any claim about recurrence: an RFC may not
assert more recurrence than it observed.

severity.description: The highest severity among this RFC's proposals.

skill_version.description:
The version recorded in the critiqued skill's own frontmatter at the
time of the run, so triage can tell whether a defect has already been
fixed since.

slug.description:
The identifier every other document uses to reference this element.

Unique across the corpus, compared without regard to letter case, and
conventionally prefixed by the document type — `adr-013`,
`container-spec-cli`, `module-document-core`.

superseded_by.description:
The document that replaces this one.

Required in practice on any document at `status: retired` — a retired
document with no resolvable successor is a dead end for anyone who
follows a reference to it.

tags.description: Free-form tags for filtering and search.

title.description:
Human-readable title. Free text.

On a promoted document this is also the document's H1, and the two are
kept in sync by hand.

type.description:
The document's classification, which selects the schema, slug pattern
and required sections that govern it.

updated_at.description:
RFC 3339 timestamp of the last substantive modification.

Validated against the text as written in the file rather than against
a parsed value, so a bare `2026-07-29` is reported as a defect instead
of being silently widened to midnight UTC by the YAML parser.

RfcSeverity.description:
How badly a run was impeded by the skill an RFC critiques.

An RFC carries the highest severity among its proposals, so that triage
can rank a queue without opening every document.

RuleId.description:
The identifier of one check, stable across releases.

Every finding names the rule that raised it, and the run report accounts
for every rule it knows about, so the identifier is the join between the
two: a caller naming a subset of checks to run names them by these
values, and reads the outcome of each back under the same value.

Identifiers are namespaced kebab-case — `slug/pattern-mismatch`,
`frontmatter/missing-property` — so the family a check belongs to is
legible without a lookup table. The shape is stated rather than
constrained because a Strata regex literal cannot contain a forward
slash.

Section.description:
A required heading, and the headings required beneath it.

Required sections are a hierarchy rather than a flat list because the
defects worth catching are about nesting: a missing `## Consequences`
and a `### Consequences` misfiled under `## Decision` are different
problems, and a flat list cannot tell them apart.

children.description: Headings required one level beneath this one.

repeated.description:
Whether the heading occurs once per instance of something in the
document rather than exactly once — one subsection per alternative
considered, for example.

Without this distinction a section tree can only describe documents of
fixed shape, and not all of the templates this framework ships are
fixed.

required.description: Whether a document of this type must contain the heading.

Severity.description:
How badly a finding bears on a run.

The three values are the whole vocabulary, and the distinction that
matters most is the third: `unverified` is not a milder failure, it is
the absence of a result. A check the tool was asked to perform and could
not run reports `unverified` rather than passing silently, because a
consumer that cannot tell the two apart will read a missing check as a
clean one.

Slug.description:
A cross-reference identifier for a specification document.

Every relationship between documents is expressed as a slug rather than a
path, so moving a file never breaks a reference. Slugs are kebab-case:
lowercase alphanumeric words joined by single hyphens.

Span.description:
A contiguous region of a document.

Byte offset and byte length are the authoritative extent, because spans
address regions *within* a line as well as whole sections — a malformed
`slug` value occupies part of a line, not the line itself. Line and
column are carried alongside for readability: they are what a human or
an agent reads in a report, and they are derived from the offset rather
than being an independent source of truth.

Lines and columns are one-based. A column counts Unicode codepoints from
the start of its line, matching the way this framework's conventions
measure width, so an em dash advances the column by one rather than by
its three UTF-8 bytes.

end_column.description: One-based codepoint column one past the last codepoint of the region.

end_line.description: One-based line on which the region ends.

length.description:
Length of the region in bytes. Zero is a valid, empty region — the
content of `---\n---` is an empty span rather than an absent one.

offset.description:
Byte offset of the first byte of the region, from the start of the
document.

start_column.description: One-based codepoint column at which the region starts.

start_line.description: One-based line on which the region starts.

SpecIndex.description:
The machine-readable description of a repository's specification corpus,
emitted to the file **specs.json** in the configured spec root.

This is the artifact CI, agents and a central architecture catalogue all
read instead of each re-deriving the corpus. It crosses a boundary, so
its shape is defined once here and generated into JSON Schema, Go and
Markdown rather than being assembled by hand in the emitter.

The model is additive by design: later features add properties to it and
to its entries under the same `schema_version`. `entries` and
`exclusions` are lists rather than maps precisely so that the emitter
owns their order and can make output byte-identical across platforms
without a change to this model.

entries.description: Every corpus member, in the order the emitter fixes.

exclusions.description: Every excluded candidate file, in the order the emitter fixes.

features.description:
Every feature any corpus member declares, with its acceptance criteria
nested beneath it, in the order the emitter fixes: by the path the
feature is written in, then by its position within that file.

A top-level collection because a feature is addressed by its slug and
not by the document that happens to hold it — nesting features under
entries would make a feature's address depend on its location, which is
what the slug exists to avoid. Criteria, by contrast, are nested inside
their feature: a criterion belongs to exactly one, and its identifier
carries that feature's code, so lookup by identifier is an index built
over this tree rather than a reason to flatten it.

input_hash.description:
A hash of everything this index was built from, written as
`sha256:` followed by lowercase hexadecimal.

This is what makes the emitted file double as a warm cache: a later
invocation recomputes the hash of the corpus's current inputs and
serves this index unchanged when the two agree, rather than
rebuilding. It is a hash of **content** — every candidate file's
repository-relative path and bytes, plus the active profile's
vocabulary — and never of modification time, so a fresh checkout
whose files all carry new timestamps and identical content is still
served warm.

Absent on an index that was not built by walking a corpus. An index
carrying no hash is never served warm; it is rebuilt.

references.description:
Every reference any corpus member makes, in the order the emitter
fixes: by the path the reference occurs in, then by its position within
that document.

One top-level collection rather than an array on each entry. A
reference is an edge; its attributes describe the edge and not either
endpoint, both directions are derived from this one list when the index
is read, and merging the indexes of two repositories into one graph is
appending rows rather than rewriting entries.

Ordering by path and then by position is what makes a document's
outbound references ordered by position in the document and the emitted
file byte-identical across platforms, in one rule.

schema_version.description:
The version of this index's schema.

Pinned to `1.0` for as long as the shape only grows. A change to the
shape of what is already here — as opposed to an addition alongside it
— updates this value and the emitted index in the same change.

workspace.description:
The workspace identifier from configuration, so that indexes emitted
by several repositories can be merged into one graph without two
documents that both declare `adr-001` colliding.

SpecsConfig.description:
The `specs.toml` file an adopting repository authors at its root.

This is the public half of the configuration contract: the surface teams
outside the CLI's own team write, and therefore the surface whose
compatibility promise costs something to keep. It is deliberately small.
A repository says which repository it is, where its documents live,
which profile is active, and a short list of house conventions —
and nothing else.

In particular there is no way to define a document type, register a
block tag, or supply a schema from here. Those belong to the profile,
and holding them back is what keeps the promise cheap: a key that was
never public cannot be broken by changing it. Promotion runs one way and
is additive, so a repository that never wrote a key it could not write
is unaffected by a later version that lets it.

Undeclared keys are a defect rather than a courtesy. A misspelled key is
far more common than a key from the future, and silently ignoring one
would let a repository believe it had configured something it had not.

conventions.description:
House conventions. Every key resolves from the active profile when
absent, so the whole table may be omitted.

profile.description: Selects the document vocabulary to check against.

workspace.description: Identifies this repository and the directory its documents live in.

Standards.description:
Cross-cutting standards, policies, guidelines or constraints that apply
across documents or components rather than to one of them.

created_at.description: RFC 3339 timestamp of the document's creation. Optional.

description.description:
A one- to two-sentence summary of what this element is and what it is
responsible for.

On C4 blueprints this is the brief description rendered on diagrams,
so it is written to be read at a glance rather than as an
introduction.

and required sections that govern it.

updated_at.description:

Validated against the text as written in the file rather than against
a parsed value, so a bare `2026-07-29` is reported as a defect instead
of being silently widened to midnight UTC by the YAML parser.

version.description:
The document's semantic version, quoted so YAML reads it as a string.

Unquoted `0.1` is a floating-point number to a YAML parser and fails
validation here — which is the intended behaviour, because `0.10` and
`0.1` are the same float and different versions.

Status.description:
The lifecycle state of a document.

State documents — blueprints, standards and contracts, which describe
what IS — use `active` and never `in-progress`. Transient change
documents, which describe a change, use `in-progress` in its place: a
change specification is implemented, not put into effect.

SystemBlueprint.description:
A C4 system blueprint: the public contracts a system provides.

The containers a system bundles are not listed here. Each container
declares the system that composes it in its own `system` property, and
the roster is derived from those inbound edges — one authoritative end,
per the Document Relationship Standard.

A system's dependency on another system is not recorded in frontmatter
at all. Where the dependency is a named interface it is a contract, and
`contracts_consumed` holds it. Where it is looser, the blueprint's own
"Consumed Systems and Contracts" section says what is depended on and
what for — which a slug list cannot, and which is what a reader actually
needs. A repository spanning more than one system is rare enough that a
frontmatter property for the untyped case would be maintained by nobody.

contracts_consumed.description:
Contract slugs this element depends on.

Named contracts only. An element's untyped collaborators are not
listed here — those are neighbour edges, and per ADR-009 they belong
to the parent that composes the elements, or to the code.

contracts_provided.description:
Contract slugs this element provides.

The interface is this element's own, so it is recorded here whatever
the element's altitude — a system's public API, a container's
service surface, a module's package API, a component's interface
where it warrants a contract document of its own.

VerificationLevel.description:
The level at which a criterion is intended to be verified.

Intent, not instruction. Nothing here executes a scenario or selects a
suite; the value records the judgement made when the criterion was
written, so that a coverage report can compare it against what tests
actually cite.

Visibility.description:
Whether an interface or module is published beyond the repository that
declares it.

Visibility governs the compatibility obligation, not the access
modifier: a public surface owes adopters a versioning policy, while an
internal one may change in lockstep with its only consumers.

name.description:
The name this repository's documents are attributed to.

It exists so that indexes emitted by several repositories can be
merged into one architecture graph without two documents that both
declare `adr-001` colliding.

root.description:
The directory the CLI walks to discover the corpus.

Resolved relative to the directory containing `specs.toml`, so a
configuration file is portable with its repository and a check run in
CI resolves the same corpus as a check run locally.
